title: SailPoint Engineer Domain 6 questions (6.2)
note: Original questions written for Delzar Certification Academy. Not from exam dumps or commercial banks; not affiliated with SailPoint.

questions.stem: Month-end brings a surge of aggregations across many tenants while other activity stays flat. Which microservice advantage lets a SaaS platform absorb this BEST?
choices: Aggregation services scale out without scaling the whole platform
Every feature shares one process, so spare capacity is used automatically
All services share one database, so no extra capacity is needed
Aggregations can be paused until the platform is redeployed
questions.answer: Aggregation services scale out without scaling the whole platform
questions.explanation: Microservices scale independently, so only the busy service gets more instances. In a monolith the whole application would have to scale together.

questions.stem: A defect causes the service that sends notification emails to crash repeatedly. In a well-designed microservice architecture, what is the expected impact?
choices: Every service stops until the email service is restarted
All requests are rolled back to keep services consistent
The tenant switches into read-only mode until the fix is deployed
Emails are delayed while other services keep working
questions.answer: Emails are delayed while other services keep working
questions.explanation: Fault isolation means a failing service degrades its own function without taking down unrelated services. A monolith is more likely to fail as a whole.

questions.stem: A SaaS vendor wants to release fixes to its certification feature several times a week without taking the rest of the product offline. Which architecture property supports this?
choices: All features are compiled and shipped together in one deployable artifact
Releases are bundled into one quarterly upgrade window
Customers install updates on their own servers
Each microservice can be deployed independently of the others
questions.answer: Each microservice can be deployed independently of the others
questions.explanation: Independent deployment lets a team ship one service without redeploying everything, which supports continuous delivery. A single artifact forces whole-product releases.

questions.stem: SailPoint's current API paths follow the pattern /service/v1/action, with each service carrying its own version. Which microservice principle does this reflect?
choices: All services must be upgraded together in one release
Services evolve and are versioned independently of each other
Clients must call one central endpoint for every operation in every service
Every service shares one schema version
questions.answer: Services evolve and are versioned independently of each other
questions.explanation: Versioning each service separately lets it change its contract on its own schedule without forcing others to move. It is the API-level view of independent deployment.

questions.stem: An architect lists properties of microservice architectures. Which one is a trade-off rather than an advantage?
choices: Independent scaling of busy services
More network calls between services, which require distributed monitoring and tracing
Isolation of failures to the affected service
Independent release cycles for each team
questions.answer: More network calls between services, which require distributed monitoring and tracing
questions.explanation: Splitting a system into services adds inter-service network traffic and makes monitoring and debugging harder. The other three options are the usual benefits.

questions.stem: Different engineering teams want to use the language and data store that best suit their service. What makes this practical in a microservice design?
choices: All services share one code base and runtime
All services read and write the same shared database tables
Each team must use the same framework version
Services interact only through defined APIs or events
questions.answer: Services interact only through defined APIs or events
questions.explanation: Because services expose only well-defined interfaces, each one can use its own technology stack. Shared tables or code bases would couple the teams again.

questions.stem: Compared with a monolith, what is a key reason a microservice-based identity platform can add a new capability with less risk?
choices: The new capability is deployed only when every other service is updated
The monolith's shared memory makes integration simpler
The new capability does not need any API
It can be built as a new service without changing unrelated code
questions.answer: It can be built as a new service without changing unrelated code
questions.explanation: New services can be added beside existing ones and integrated through APIs, limiting the change's blast radius. In a monolith any change means rebuilding and redeploying the whole application.

questions.stem: An integration must change only the description of an existing ISC object without resending the whole object. Which request style fits BEST?
choices: PUT with only the description field in the body
PATCH with a JSON Patch body, sent as application/json-patch+json
POST with the full object to the collection
GET with the new description as a query parameter
questions.answer: PATCH with a JSON Patch body, sent as application/json-patch+json
questions.explanation: PATCH with JSON Patch operations changes specific fields and leaves the rest untouched. A PUT replaces the whole resource, so omitted fields can be cleared or rejected.

questions.stem: A script updates an object with PUT but sends only two of its fields. The object loses several other settings. Why?
choices: PUT only works when the object is first deleted
PUT merges fields but drops any that are null
PUT replaces the entire resource with the body that was sent
PUT is not supported by REST APIs
questions.answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with the body that was sent
questions.explanation: PUT means replace: the body becomes the new representation of the resource. For partial changes, use PATCH.

questions.stem: A network timeout leaves a script unsure whether its last request reached the API. Which request is safe to repeat without creating a duplicate?
choices: A POST that creates a new object
A DELETE of a specific object by its ID
A POST that submits a new access request
A POST that starts a new aggregation
questions.answer: A DELETE of a specific object by its ID
questions.explanation: DELETE, like GET and PUT, is idempotent: repeating it leaves the same end state. Each POST shown creates something new, so repeating it can duplicate work.

questions.stem: A call that worked yesterday now returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized, while the same client gets data from other endpoints after fetching a new token. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: The access token used for the call had expired
The client lacks the scope that the endpoint requires
The requested object no longer exists
The request body was not valid JSON
questions.answer: The access token used for the call had expired
questions.explanation: 401 means authentication failed, typically a missing, invalid or expired token, and a fresh token solves it. A missing scope gives 403, and a missing object gives 404.

questions.stem: A personal access token authenticates successfully, but a call to create a source returns HTTP 403 Forbidden. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: The token has expired and must be refreshed
The source name contains spaces
The API is temporarily rate limiting the client after a burst of calls
The token's user level or scopes do not allow creating sources
questions.answer: The token's user level or scopes do not allow creating sources
questions.explanation: 403 means the caller is authenticated but not authorized for the operation. Expired tokens give 401 and rate limiting gives 429.

questions.stem: A script sends GET for an identity using an ID copied from another tenant and receives HTTP 404 Not Found. What does this indicate?
choices: No resource with that ID exists in the tenant being called
The token is missing from the request's Authorization header
The request is valid but is still being processed
The request was throttled by the API gateway
questions.answer: No resource with that ID exists in the tenant being called
questions.explanation: 404 means the requested resource could not be found at that path, which is expected for an ID from a different tenant. A missing token gives 401 and throttling gives 429.

questions.stem: A script triggers a long-running operation and receives HTTP 202 Accepted. What should it do next?
choices: Treat the operation as finished and successful
Resend the request, because 202 means the API ignored it
Track the returned task or status until it completes
Assume the operation failed and roll back
questions.answer: Track the returned task or status until it completes
questions.explanation: 202 means the request was accepted for asynchronous processing and is not finished yet. The script should poll the status it was given rather than resend it.

questions.stem: A nightly integration must call ISC APIs with no person present. Which OAuth 2.0 flow fits?
choices: Authorization code, requiring an administrator to sign in each night
Implicit flow, returning the token in the browser
Client credentials, exchanging a client ID and secret at the tenant's token endpoint
Basic authentication with an administrator's user name and password
questions.answer: Client credentials, exchanging a client ID and secret at the tenant's token endpoint
questions.explanation: Client credentials is the machine-to-machine flow: the integration posts its client ID and secret to the token endpoint and receives an access token. Authorization code needs a user present.

questions.stem: An engineer creates a personal access token to automate a task. Whose permissions does the token carry?
choices: Those of the user who created it, further limited by the scopes chosen
Full tenant administrator rights, no matter which user originally created it
Only read access, because personal tokens cannot change data
The permissions of the source owner of each object called
questions.answer: Those of the user who created it, further limited by the scopes chosen
questions.explanation: A personal access token acts as the identity that owns it, so it can never exceed that user's level, and scopes narrow it further. It is not an automatic administrator credential.

questions.stem: How should a script present an ISC access token when calling the APIs?
choices: As a query parameter named token in every URL
In the Authorization header as a Bearer token
In the request body of every GET request
As a cookie set by the Admin UI
questions.answer: In the Authorization header as a Bearer token
questions.explanation: ISC APIs expect the OAuth access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Tokens in URLs leak into logs and browser history.

questions.stem: A long-running sync script begins getting 401 responses partway through each run. What is the BEST design fix?
choices: Hard-code a token generated in the Admin UI into the script
Retry the same call with the same token until it succeeds
Switch to a user's password in each call
Request a new token when the current one expires
questions.answer: Request a new token when the current one expires
questions.explanation: Access tokens are short-lived, so a robust client requests a fresh token when it expires. Retrying with an expired token will keep failing.

questions.stem: A team is creating a personal access token for a reporting job that only reads identities and accounts. Which practice is BEST?
choices: Grant every scope so the job never fails later
Share one token across all teams to reduce sprawl
Grant only the read scopes needed and keep the secret in a vault
Paste the secret into the job's source code repository
questions.answer: Grant only the read scopes needed and keep the secret in a vault
questions.explanation: Least-privilege scopes limit what a leaked token can do, and a vault keeps the secret out of code. Shared, all-powerful tokens destroy accountability.

questions.stem: An engineer is calling the ISC token endpoint for the client credentials flow. Which request is correct?
choices: POST to the tenant's API host at /oauth/token with grant_type client_credentials
GET to the Admin UI home page with the secret in the URL
POST to the virtual appliance with the client secret
PUT to the search endpoint with the client ID in the body
questions.answer: POST to the tenant's API host at /oauth/token with grant_type client_credentials
questions.explanation: Tokens are issued by the tenant's OAuth token endpoint on the API host. The VA and other API endpoints do not issue tokens.

questions.stem: A script must list about 1,200 access profiles through a standard list endpoint. How should it page through them?
choices: Use limit up to 250 and raise offset until no records return
Set limit to 1200 to get everything in one call
Call the endpoint repeatedly without parameters until the list changes
Use searchAfter on the list endpoint
questions.answer: Use limit up to 250 and raise offset until no records return
questions.explanation: List endpoints return at most 250 records per page, so the script uses limit and offset to walk the collection. searchAfter is for the Search API.

questions.stem: A developer calls a list endpoint with offset=1 and limit=20. Which records come back?
choices: The second through the twenty-first record
The second page of twenty records
Records one through twenty, counting from one
Twenty records starting at a random position
questions.answer: The second through the twenty-first record
questions.explanation: offset is record-based and zero-indexed, so offset=1 skips only the first record. It is not a page number.

questions.stem: A dashboard needs the total number of identities matching a filter without downloading them all. What should the call include?
choices: limit=0, then count the records returned
sorters=total, then read the first record
count=true, then read the X-Total-Count response header
offset=-1, then read the last record
questions.answer: count=true, then read the X-Total-Count response header
questions.explanation: count=true returns the total size of the filtered collection in the X-Total-Count header. Because it costs performance, it should be sent only when the value is used.

questions.stem: A script must list only the identities whose name starts with Raj, newest first. Which query parameters fit?
choices: filters=name eq "Raj*" with sorters=created
filters=name sw "Raj" with sorters=-created
filters=name co "Raj" with sorters=+created
filters=startsWith(name, "Raj") with sorters=desc(created)
questions.answer: filters=name sw "Raj" with sorters=-created
questions.explanation: sw is the starts-with operator, and a leading minus in sorters makes the sort descending. eq does an exact match, and co matches the text anywhere in the value.

questions.stem: A filter value contains the # character, and the API returns unexpected results. What should the developer do?
choices: Remove the filters parameter and sort instead
Wrap the whole URL in single quotation marks
URL-encode the character in the query string
Send the filter in an X-Filter header
questions.answer: URL-encode the character in the query string
questions.explanation: Characters such as # and & have special meaning in URLs and must be encoded, for example # as %23. Otherwise the query string is cut short.

questions.stem: A script needs every identity in a tenant with 60,000 identities using the Search API. Which paging approach is recommended?
choices: Increase offset by 10,000 for each call
Set limit to 60,000 in one request
Repeat the same query until the results it returns stop changing
Sort by id and pass the last id from each page in searchAfter
questions.answer: Sort by id and pass the last id from each page in searchAfter
questions.explanation: Search pagination uses sort on id with searchAfter set to the last record's id. Offset-based paging is not the recommended way to page through large search results.

questions.stem: A Search API call should return identities in the Finance department. Which request is correctly formed?
choices: A GET with the query in the URL path and no request body
A POST with indices set to identities and a query such as attributes.department:Finance
A PUT with the identity IDs to search for in the body
A DELETE that removes every identity outside Finance
questions.answer: A POST with indices set to identities and a query such as attributes.department:Finance
questions.explanation: Search is a POST whose JSON body names the indices and holds the query string. The other methods do not run searches.

questions.stem: An engineer needs identities across the tenant that hold a specific entitlement and are in a given department. Which API approach is MOST efficient?
choices: List every identity, then fetch each identity's access one by one
One Search API query across the identities index
List every source and read each account separately
Export a CSV from each source and join the files by hand
questions.answer: One Search API query across the identities index
questions.explanation: Search runs queries across indexed identity data in a single call. Walking every identity or account multiplies calls and quickly hits rate limits.

questions.stem: Immediately after an identity is updated, a Search API query does not yet show the new value, though a direct GET on the identity does. What is the MOST likely reason?
choices: The Search API caches results for each client for one day
The identity was updated in a different tenant
The query used an operator that is not supported
The search index is refreshed shortly after changes
questions.answer: The search index is refreshed shortly after changes
questions.explanation: Search reads an index that is refreshed after changes, so there can be a short delay, while direct object endpoints read the current record. Scripts that verify changes should allow for it.

questions.stem: What is the default number of records a Search API call returns per request when limit is not specified?
choices: Up to 10,000 records
Up to 250 records
Up to 50 records
Up to 1,000 records per page
questions.answer: Up to 10,000 records
questions.explanation: The Search endpoint defaults to and allows up to 10,000 records per page, unlike list endpoints, which allow 250. Larger result sets are paged with searchAfter.

questions.stem: A bulk script receives HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. What is the correct client behaviour?
choices: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the call succeeds
Wait the seconds given in Retry-After, then retry
Request a new token, because 429 means it expired
Switch to a different tenant to continue
questions.answer: Wait the seconds given in Retry-After, then retry
questions.explanation: 429 signals the rate limit was reached, and Retry-After gives the seconds to wait. A tight loop keeps the client throttled, and the token is still valid.

questions.stem: Through the API gateway, what is SailPoint's default API rate limit?
choices: 100 requests per tenant every hour
10,000 requests per user every minute
100 requests per client ID and API version every 10 seconds
One request per second for each endpoint
questions.answer: 100 requests per client ID and API version every 10 seconds
questions.explanation: The documented default is 100 requests per client_id and API version per 10 seconds, with 429 returned when it is exceeded. Clients should be designed to stay inside it.

questions.stem: A developer wants to call an endpoint marked experimental. What must each request include?
choices: The X-SailPoint-Experimental header set to true
A query parameter named beta set to yes
A personal access token with the admin scope
A body field named experimental with the value true
questions.answer: The X-SailPoint-Experimental header set to true
questions.explanation: Experimental endpoints require the X-SailPoint-Experimental header with the value true on each request; it is how the client opts in to experimental behaviour. Query parameters, scopes or body fields do not do this.

questions.stem: A team is starting a new integration and sees Beta, V3, yearly versioned paths and the newer /service/v1/action paths. Which choice is BEST for long-term support?
choices: Build against Beta, since it gets new features first
Build against V3, since it will never be deprecated
Build against the newer service-versioned paths
Mix all versions to spread the risk
questions.answer: Build against the newer service-versioned paths
questions.explanation: SailPoint is deprecating Beta, V3 and yearly versions in favour of independent service versions, so new work should target the newer paths. Legacy versions have announced end-of-support dates.

questions.stem: A nightly job makes thousands of small list calls and keeps hitting the rate limit. Which redesign BEST reduces throttling?
choices: Create many API clients and rotate between them
Remove all waiting so the job finishes before the limit resets
Send every call with count=true
Use larger pages or Search so fewer calls return the same data
questions.answer: Use larger pages or Search so fewer calls return the same data
questions.explanation: Fetching more data per call reduces request volume within the limit. Rotating clients to get around the limit is poor practice, and count=true adds load without reducing calls.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to automate ISC tasks in PowerShell without hand-building every HTTP request. What does SailPoint provide for this?
choices: A built-in PowerShell console in the Admin UI
Direct database access for PowerShell scripts
A PowerShell SDK that wraps the ISC APIs
A PowerShell module that runs only on the virtual appliance
questions.answer: A PowerShell SDK that wraps the ISC APIs
questions.explanation: SailPoint publishes SDKs, including one for PowerShell, along with a CLI, so scripts can call the APIs without building raw requests. There is no direct database access to a SaaS tenant.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a client credentials integration with ISC in order.
items: Create an API credential, such as a personal access token, with only the scopes needed
Post the client ID and secret to the tenant's token endpoint with grant_type client_credentials
Receive the access token in the response
Call the API with the token in the Authorization: Bearer header
Request a new token when the current one expires
questions.explanation: The credential is created first, exchanged for a short-lived access token, and then the token is presented on each call. Expired tokens are replaced rather than reused.

questions.stem: Match each HTTP status code to what it tells an ISC API client.

pairs.match: The token is missing, invalid or expired
The caller is authenticated but lacks the rights or scopes
No resource exists at that path or ID
The rate limit was hit; wait for Retry-After

targets_extra: The request was accepted for asynchronous processing
questions.explanation: 401 and 403 separate authentication from authorization, 404 means the target was not found, and 429 means throttling. Asynchronous acceptance is 202, which is not listed.

questions.stem: Which TWO are advantages of a microservice architecture over a monolith?
choices: Each service can be scaled on its own
A failure in one service is less likely to stop the whole system
Fewer network calls between components
One shared database that makes schema changes simpler
A single deployment that releases every feature together
answers: Each service can be scaled on its own
A failure in one service is less likely to stop the whole system
questions.explanation: Independent scaling and fault isolation are core microservice benefits. Microservices add network calls, avoid one shared database and deploy independently, so the other options describe monoliths or trade-offs.
